title: Position: Medical AI Neglects Real Treatment Outcomes
claim: Automated label validation against regulatory documents can accept a wrong answer, so benchmark ground truth for treatment outcomes is unreliable.
layout: 1 panel, top-to-bottom, green and red highlights on a case vignette
description: A single rounded-corner box holds a medical multiple-choice question. At the top is a clinical case vignette, set in labeled paragraphs: Case, Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Findings, Genetic Investigation and Declined Testing. These describe a 28-year-old woman with chronic pancreatitis and a CFTR gene variant. Key evidence phrases, such as the age and sex, the diagnosis, no family history and the CFTR variant, are highlighted in light green. Below the vignette is the question: characterize the utility of ivacaftor for resolving this patient's pancreatitis. Four answer options, A to D, sit in two columns. Option C, the correct one, is highlighted green. Option D, the wrongly accepted one, is highlighted red. The eye goes first to the colored highlights and the contrast between C and D.
caption: A \hlred{mislabeling} that occurs when regulatory documents and LLMs are used to (synthetically) validate labels for benchmarks, in a manner reminiscent of [ref] and [ref]. This question derives from a real, published case report in which ivacaftor resolved a patient's pancreatitis [ref]. The correct answer is (C); the supporting evidence for this answer is \hlgreen{highlighted green}, and their connection is explained in the main text. Unfortunately, the \hlred{incorrect answer (D)} passes both of the automated correctness checks of [ref], which are based on the FDA product label for ivacaftor. The fundamental problem is that regulatory documents, such as drug labels, are not intended to provide comprehensive ground truth for treatment outcomes. Note that the RxQA dataset is additionally verified by pharmacists, and for clarity, whereas TreatmentPC is not.
abstract: Medical AI has rapidly improved its ability to perform diagnostic and prognostic tasks that lead to treatment decisions. But understanding of treatment itself is still inadequately trained and evaluated, using human opinions and syntheses (especially texts such as biomedical publications and clinical practice guidelines) rather than actual underlying data on treatment outcomes. This neglect seriously limits the potential of medical AI, and is already causing deficiencies in both frontier models and major benchmarks, as argued in this position paper. Real treatment outcomes, drawn from sources such as observational databases and randomized experiments, should be substantially incorporated into both training and evaluation. Improving these outcomes should be reemphasized as the downstream goal of all medical AI.
